display_title: Official Review of Paper480 by Reviewer uYxa

content.summary_of_the_paper: The purpose of the paper is to understand the existence of adversarial examples for the modern artificial neural network. Specifically, first, the paper introduces a novel approach in describing the submanifold of samples and the decision boundaries using a complex-valued hypothesis and gives a necessary condition for the hypothesis being robust to adversarial examples. Second, this paper gives an explanation for the transfer of adversarial examples between analytic hypotheses. Finally, this paper tries to propose methods for mitigating the affect of adversarial examples by generalizing the linear maximum margin classification to a certain hypothesis class.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
1. Novelty: The angle of the paper is novel. The paper tries to explain the existence of adversarial examples by analyzing the hypotheses using complex analysis tools. According to this paper, the existence of adversarial examples seems to be caused by certain analytic properties of the hypothesis class. And very importantly, the hypothesis class can unify some of the proposals raised in previous works. 
2. Significance: This paper might propose a possible direction for a general mathematical theory for adversarial robustness. There have been many good application work in the field of adversarial robustness. However, from the theoretical side, researchers are still in search of a unified theory to explain the existence and behavior of adversarial examples.

Weakness:
1. Rigorousness: This paper is a purely theoretical work in my opinion (though it has numerical simulations). Unfortunately, I did not find the claims in the paper is rigorous enough for a theoretical work. Specifically, the paper made several strong claims without rigorous mathematical analysis. For example, in section 2, the paper tries to explain the transfer phenomenon of adversarial examples from the lens of holomorphic optimal Bayes classifier. But there is no theorem/proof or detailed analysis, making the claim not convincing at all. Another example, in section 3, the paper lists the primal and dual problem for learning the maximum margin classifier, but there is again no rigorous mathematical derivation. Although the paper states that its claims are evident from the definition, as a reader, I did not find it evident at all. 
To sum up, the problem of the current presentation of this paper is that I cannot tell which parts are rigorous theorems and which parts are just intuitions. Therefore, I am very concerned about the rigorousness of this paper, and I do not think it qualifies as a theoretical work.
I recommend the authors to 1) state clearly which parts are rigorous math and which are just intuitions/illustrations 2) summarize all the rigorous parts into mathematical theorems, 3) then give rigorous proofs.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Although the angle of the paper is novel and the problem considered is very significant, I do not think the paper is rigorous enough.
Therefore, my current recommendation is rejection.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors attempt to account for the existence of adversarial examples by proposing a model they call the diverging derivative model.
content.main_review:
I have made an earnest attempt to read thoroughly the main text of the submission.

The authors mention several shortcomings of their methods in the paper such as reliance on a polynomial function class. However I have several more fundamental issues with the approach which I found unaddressed in the paper:

The motivation for holomorphic functions here is unclear. For example, what benefit is there to the topology specifically of $\mathbb C$ modelling adversarial examples that is absent from $\mathbb{R}^2$?

How do holomorphic hypothesis functions work? What is the decision criterion when your hypothesis is $\mathbb C$-valued? Have holomorphic hypotheses classes been studied in the literature? Is the approach here consistent with any other treatments?

Several times the sets $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal C$ are described as submanifolds. Do they indeed possess topologies having a manifold structure (locally Euclidean, preferably smooth)? Or is this an assumption that has been made. It is unclear.

For a paper that claims to eliminate adversarial examples, I was expecting a theorem or statement at some point. What is the central insight you are able to deliver through your theory of diverging derivatives?

Finally, editorially, the authors should attempt to include all necessary notation and definitions as part of the paper. At least one symbol $A^2(\Omega)$ is defined only in the appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes what might be an interesting way to study the existence of adversarial examples. However I believe in its present form the exposition here is inappropriate for a venue such as ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a model based on holomorphic functions to explain the existence and transfer of adversarial examples.
content.main_review:
Honestly speaking, I did not understand the paper. Despite the seemingly interesting idea, I find the paper quite hard to read. Observations from evidence, novel ideas and rigorous mathematical reasoning are all mixed together. It's very hard to spell out what is what. Answering the following questions in future versions may help.

The only reason the authors use complex variables and holomorphic functions is that an earlier work showed that S and C are perpendicular in a linear classifier. On the other hand, adversarial robustness is not interesting for linear classifiers. So why would complex variables help? I couldn't find a compelling reason for that.

Equation 6 and 8 are mysterious. Why does Newton iteration yields the shortest curve?

Why does $\mathcal{H}_n^\Omega$ have a finite VC dimension? Isn't it a class of complex-valued functions?

The appearance of gradient in equation 9 seems to be based on an intuitive idea rather than a rigorous proof? There are so many such cases in the paper that I have trouble treating it as a theory paper despite the seemingly deep nature.

The title is a bit misleading as the paper doesn't actually use any feature of several complex variables which is absent in one complex variable.

What happens when the domain is the entire space? There won't be a Bergman space in that case. Are domains other than poly-disk interesting? Is the Bergman kernel for the ball known?
content.summary_of_the_review: In its current form I don't think it's readable for ICLR audience, so I cannot recommend it. However, I think the idea is quite novel, so I encourage the authors polish and further develop it, and I look forward to the future versions of this paper. I'd also love to see other reviewers' opinion.

content.comment:
Thank you for the time and helpful comments. We hope that the revised version will be more understandable.

"The only reason the authors use complex variables and holomor..."

Using holomorphicity, we generalize the result of Tanay & Griffin to the case of analytic hypotheses. We tried to address the issue by elaborating on the use of holomorphic functions and the necessity of their use. We have changed the organization of the paper to make it more readable and to put the important parts of the proposal in formal theorems. The proofs could be found in the appendix and we make use of holomorphicity of the hypothesis in the proofs quite a lot.

"Equation 6 and 8 are mysterious. Why does Newton iteration yields the shortest curve?"

We have changed the presentation of the proposal in regards to the shortest paths. We have added theorems 3.1 and 3.2 in the revised version of the paper which will hopefully resolve the mysteries.

"Why does $\mathcal{H}_n^\Omega$ has a finite VC dimension? Isn't it a class of complex-valued functions?

We have added theorem 2.2 to better present this part of the proposal. The proof of the theorem in the appendix should clear things up. Just keep in mind that we are using the real and imaginary parts of a complex-valued hypothesis separately. So, we do not need to provide a definition for the VC-dimension of a complex-valued function.

"The appearance of gradient in equation 9 seem.."

We hope that the revised version of the paper sounds more rigorous. We have added theorems 3.1 and 3.2 in the revised version of the paper which will hopefully resolve this issue.

"The title is a bit misleading as the paper doesn't actually use any feature of seve..."

While we understand your concern, we have to disagree on this issue. On the contrary, we think it would be misleading not to mention several complex variables at all. It is true that we do not make use of aspects of the theory that are unique to several variables in this paper, but it was necessary to make sure that the concepts used does generalize to several complex variables. Similarly, if one wants to further this proposal, she needs to take into account the differences in the analysis of one and several complex variables. 

"What happens when the domain is the entire space? There won't be a Bergman space in that case. Are domains other than poly-disk interesting? Is the Bergman kernel for the ball known?"

We have elaborated on the issue of the domains a little more in page 3, after theorem 2.2, of the revised paper. We mention the domains of holomorphy for the reader to follow up on if she was interested.  As of this moment, we have only used the poly-disk as a domain. But, we believe that the ball and the anulus would be of interest in the future. The Bergman kernel of the ball is already known and some approximations of the Bergman kernel of the annulus could be found in the literature.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose using complex functions to analyze and understand the phenomenon of adversarial examples. They use holomorphic functions and analyze the corresponding maximum margin classifier. Through synchronization they turn an $\ell^2$ regularization into a regularization of the derivative, which they argue promotes robustness. They then include experimental results as evidence for their claims.
content.main_review:
It is unclear what is gained by using complex variables. Problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are extended to $\mathbb{C}^d$. But then it is not clear what is gained if all of the samples are in the real submanifold. The paper then proceeds by considering problems naturally in $\mathbb{C}^d$ (for which no applications are given).

The explanation given for why adversarial examples transfer is that "all holomorphic hypotheses are forced to converge to the orthogonal projection of the optimal Bayes classifier". This is at odds with their proposal for a way to mitigate adversarial examples, since the projection of the optimal model "is independent of the details of implementation or training".

The experiments are on relatively small data sets, and not many results are given. As a result, they are unconvincing.

The use of synchronization to regularize the derivative is an interesting idea.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is unclear what is gained by using the framework proposed in the paper. The experimental results are unconvincing.

display_title: Explaining the reasons behind the extension to $\mathbb(C)$ and rebuttal of inconsistency in the definition of holomorphic optimal Bayes clasifier

content.title: Explaining the reasons behind the extension to $\mathbb(C)$ and rebuttal of inconsistency in the definition of holomorphic optimal Bayes clasifier
content.comment:
The reason behind the extension of the input domain to the complex plane is not that the samples are complex or that they need to be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$. As we mention in the paper, the reason is to provide space in the 1D case for the decision boundary to expand outside the submanifold of the samples, enabling geometrical interpretations. Also, we are not proposing that there is a need to complexify the training samples either. Even though it is true that all of the natural samples are real vectors, it is not true that all real vectors are natural samples (consider an adversarial example). As a result, when we use a real-valued hypothesis, we have no way to determine the submanifold of the samples, and this information is lost. The significance of complex input is only realized when we accept that the hypothesis cannot be real-valued on $\mathbb{R}^d$. In that case, complex input vectors would exist that are considered to be "natural" by the definition we have chosen for the imaginary part of the hypothesis. Nevertheless, the existence of these complex vectors does not affect the results in our paper. We mention in the conclusion part of the paper that we are considering the use of complex-valued hypothesis in designing defense mechanisms by projecting the test sample into $\mathcal{S}$ in the inference time which we think naturally implies that $\mathbb{R}^d$ was not to be considered as the submanifold of the samples, even though all of the natural samples are real vectors. Thus, we do not believe that there is a need to provide an application for problems in $\mathbb{C}$ since they are irrelevant to our discussion.

Regarding the apparent paradox in the definitions, the reviewer has left out an important part of the proposal. In our proposal, we assert that the holomorphic optimal Bayes classifier is "the infinite sample limit of any learning rule on the space of holomorphic hypotheses". By which we mean that if we show infinite samples to any sane learning rule (robust or not), the resulting classifier would be the holomorphic optimal Bayes classifier since it is the closest holomorphic hypothesis to the optimal Bayes classifier. Otherwise, the optimality of the optimal Bayes classifier would be challenged. But since we do not have access to infinite samples, we have to find a learning rule that stays robust when there are only a finite number of training samples available. Hence, we propose the holomorphic maximum margin classifier in the paper which inherits its robustness from the fact that it is holomorphic and maximum margin on $\mathcal{S}$. We mention in the paper (page 3) that holomorphicity is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for robustness. If there are any doubts on the robustness of a maximum margin learning rule, we can provide references in the literature that explain this issue.

The reviewer also mentions that the experimental results are unconvincing. The reason behind the small experiments is that we have yet to find an efficient way to implement the proposal for the standard datasets in the literature. We have mentioned this shortcoming in the conclusion part of the paper and dedicated Appendix C to this issue.

content.title: Extension Motivation
content.comment:
Thanks for your response. However, I'm still a bit confused about the motivation.

In the 1D case, the submanifold of the samples is the real line (how is this better than the real-valued hypothesis in determining the submanifold of samples?), and the reason for providing space is to expand the decision boundary. I still don't understand what is gained by expanding the decision boundary in this way. In the paper it is stated that "to define the distance between a training sample and the decision boundary in the general case, we need to find the shortest curve that starts from the sample and ends somewhere on the submanifold of the decision boundary", where this shortest curve lies on the submanifold of samples. This would just be the distance on the real line from the sample to a decision point (a 0D boundary). What useful geometrical interpretations does making the decision boundary 1D enable, when the only relevant aspect is the 0D boundary?

content.title: Describing the relevant changes in the paper to the review
content.comment:
Thank you for your time. We have revised the paper and made some changes to the organization of the paper. Hopefully it is more accessible now. Theorem 2.1 in the revised version tries to better explain the need for complex variables. We have also added some comments to the conclusion part and elaborated more on the reasons why similar theorems and analysis could not be done using real variables and real analytic functions.

"What useful geometrical interpretations does making the decision boundary 1D enable, when the only relevant aspect is the 0D boundary?"
In the proof of theorem 2.1 we show that when we force robustness (in the sense of boundary tilting perspective), the hypothesis is either constant or the domain of the hypothesis is a subset of the complex plane. Consequently, reducing the domain of the hypothesis to a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ would make the hypothesis trivial and uninteresting.
